scorecard.note: Add a clearer narrative arc that links the otters' comeback to the carbon benefit, making the story feel like a progression rather than three separate facts.

storyboard.ears: A tiny surviving group became the start of a coastal recovery.
California sea otters fell to 50 by the 1930s. The population survived from a tiny remnant.
storyboard.evidence: U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service | California sea otter population, before the fur trade vs the 1930s low point | https://www.fws.gov/ | 2026-11-13

storyboard.ears: California sea otters later reached 3,000. The remnant grew into today's recovered population.
storyboard.evidence: U.S. Geological Survey / California Department of Fish and Wildlife | California sea otter population recovery, 1930s to today | https://www.usgs.gov/ | 2026-11-13

storyboard.ears: Otter-protected kelp could store 8.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide yearly. Their range carries measurable carbon potential.
storyboard.evidence: Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment | Potential CO2 stored by otter-protected kelp forests, North Pacific range | https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/journal/15409309 | 2026-11-13

storyboard.ears: Protecting sea otters preserves their recovery and the kelp carbon linked to them.
